name: Vallabhbhai Patel
role: Indian independence leader, first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister of India (1875-1950)
summary: Patel is read here through his own words in the Constituent Assembly, his letters of 1945-50 and reprinted speeches. The record shows a firm opponent of separate electorates and of nationalising industry quickly, who kept Scheduled Caste reservation, backed Hindi with a ten-year English period, and banned the RSS after Gandhi's murder. Most statements stay unanswered because the sources read do not state a position.

sources.title: Constituent Assembly Debates, 27 August 1947 (Advisory Committee report on minority safeguards, moved by Patel)
sources.author: Vallabhbhai Patel (mover); Constituent Assembly of India
sources.usedFor: Joint electorates, no weightage, reservation by population, reservation in services for Anglo-Indians and Scheduled Castes.

sources.title: Constituent Assembly Debates, 25 May 1949 (Patel moves the Advisory Committee report)
sources.author: Vallabhbhai Patel (mover); Constituent Assembly of India
sources.usedFor: Dropping reservations for religious minorities, keeping them for the Scheduled Castes for ten years, a state based on nationalistic principles.

sources.title: Sardar Patel's Correspondence 1945-50 (ed. Durga Das), vols 2, 3 and 6, Internet Archive full text
sources.author: Vallabhbhai Patel
sources.usedFor: Letter to Munshi of 19 August 1949 on Hindi and English; 1946 letter on nationalisation; chronology of 1946 acts; privy purse and compensation letters of August 1949; Hindu Code Bill letters (checked, nothing stated by Patel on its merits).

sources.title: Life and Work of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (tribute volume with reprinted speeches), Internet Archive
sources.author: Vallabhbhai Patel (speeches reprinted); editors
sources.usedFor: Speeches on Kashmir and plebiscite, the idea of a Hindu State, and labour disputes settled by arbitration.

sources.title: Vallabhbhai Patel, Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: In August 1949 he agreed with the colleague who wrote that the pledges on privy purses must be honoured; the covenants he negotiated kept the rulers' purses, though the princely states themselves were ended.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: After Gandhi's murder he agreed to Nehru's proposal to ban the RSS, the Muslim National Guard and the Khaksars, and as Home Minister enforced the ban.

communal-electorates.rationale: As chairman of the minorities committee he brought a report to the Assembly that ended separate electorates; he told it that there had been unanimity that there should be no more separate electorates and that joint electorates should follow, and in 1949 denounced the separate communal electorate motion as a legacy of the Muslim League.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Speaking in Calcutta in January 1948 he said that India had made plain that a plebiscite should be the deciding factor in Kashmir, while adding that none could be held while fighting went on.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: He moved the 1949 revision to put the Constitution on the principles of a genuine democratic state based purely on nationalistic principles and said religion was being used as a cloak for political purposes.

population-transfer.rationale: His chronology records that he spurned Jinnah's proposal for an exchange of population; the source is an editor's chronology, not his words.

property-fundamental.rationale: In August 1949 he wrote that he took the same view as his correspondent on compensation and that the formula making compensation justiciable for all property, zamindari included, met his views better than the party compromise.

public-ownership.rationale: Britannica reports that he belittled the usefulness of adapting socialist ideas and believed in free enterprise. In 1946 he told the Central Legislative Assembly that it was not desirable to go fast on nationalisation, and wrote to a Bombay premier that ministers talking of nationalising sugar and textiles created insecurity and discouraged individual initiative; he accepted state control of industry in principle.

reserved-seats-excluded-groups.rationale: In 1949 he moved to drop reservation of seats for religious minorities, but accepted the amendment to keep it for the Scheduled Castes for ten years, and in 1947 he reported reservation in services for the Anglo-Indians and Scheduled Castes as deserving special consideration.

single-official-language.rationale: In a letter to Munshi of 19 August 1949 he proposed Hindi in Devanagari script as the national or official language, English kept alongside it for ten years and then replaced completely by Hindi.

notes: First audit. Read the Constituent Assembly debates of 27 August 1947 and 25-26 May 1949, volumes 1-7 of his Select Correspondence and the Life and Work speeches volume, searching by theme: electorates and reservations, Hindi and English, nationalisation, labour, Kashmir and plebiscite, cow protection, the Hindu Code Bill, privy purses and compensation, the RSS ban. On cow slaughter the letters are addressed to him, not written by him. On the Hindu Code Bill he reported the party's decision to support it but stated no view on the merits. On strikes he urged arbitration without proposing a law. Those stay null. The answers are few and the uncertainty rule is not met; none of the confidences was raised to pass it.
